title: Free-Body Diagrams, Gravity Lever-Arm Torque & Gear Speed/Torque Power Scaling

blocks.x: This is the bridge module before Step 1.3 (`02-mechanics.T1.03`). Before sizing a robot arm motor or computing $N^2$ reflected inertia in Step 1.3, you need to isolate a link in a **Free-Body Diagram (FBD)**, calculate how gravity torque varies with shoulder angle ($\tau_g = m g L_{\text{com}} \cos\theta$), and understand how a gearbox or timing belt trades speed for torque while conserving mechanical power ($P = \tau \omega$). Already know this? Take the Skip test or the Ladder Gate test in section 7 first.

blocks.caption: Gravity torque is a cosine: largest with the link horizontal, zero with it vertical.

blocks.x: Hold a heavy dumbbell straight out at shoulder height ($\theta = 0\text{ rad}$ horizontal): your shoulder muscles burn because gravity acts at the full horizontal lever arm $L\cos(0) = L$. Now raise your arm straight overhead ($\theta = \pi/2\text{ rad}$ vertical): the dumbbell rests directly over your shoulder pivot with zero horizontal lever arm ($L\cos(\pi/2) = 0$), requiring zero holding torque! Drawing a **Free-Body Diagram (FBD)** means cutting the link free from the rest of the world and drawing arrows for every force and torque acting on it so nothing is forgotten. And a **gearbox** with ratio $N:1$ acts as a rotary lever: much like a $10\times$ crowbar moves your hand $10\times$ farther to multiply force by $10\times$, an $N:1$ gear reducer spins the motor shaft $N$ times faster than the output joint while multiplying output torque by $N\times$.

items.x: **Free-Body Diagram & Static Equilibrium ($\sum F = 0,\ \sum \tau = 0$):** For a rigid body to remain stationary ($\ddot{x} = 0, \ddot{\theta} = 0$), the vector sum of external forces $\sum F_x = 0, \sum F_y = 0$ (in $\text{N}$) and the sum of torques about any pivot $\sum \tau_z = 0$ (in $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$) must vanish.

**Planar Link Gravity Holding Torque ($\tau_g(\theta)$):** For a link of mass $m$ ($\text{kg}$) whose center of mass lies at distance $L_{\text{com}}$ ($\text{m}$) from the joint pivot at angle $\theta$ ($\text{rad}$) measured from the horizontal $+x$-axis, gravity $m g$ acts straight down ($-y$), creating perpendicular lever arm $r_\perp = L_{\text{com}}\cos\theta$. The joint torque required to hold the link plus a tip payload $m_{\text{tip}}$ at length $L$ is:

blocks.x: Substituting $m = 0.40\text{ kg}$, $L_{\text{com}} = 0.10\text{ m}$, $m_{\text{tip}} = 0.50\text{ kg}$, $L = 0.20\text{ m}$, $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$, and $\theta = 0\text{ rad}$ gives $\tau_{\max} = (0.04 + 0.10)(9.81)\cos(0) = 1.3734\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$.

items.x: **Gear Ratio Speed/Torque Scaling and Power Conservation:** For an ideal gear or belt reduction of ratio $N = \omega_{\text{motor}} / \omega_{\text{load}} = r_{\text{load}} / r_{\text{motor}}$ with efficiency $\eta \in (0, 1]$:

blocks.x: Substituting $N = 8.0$, $\eta = 1.0$, $\tau_{\text{motor}} = 0.25\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$, and $\omega_{\text{motor}} = 160\text{ rad/s}$ gives $\tau_{\text{load}} = 2.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$, $\omega_{\text{load}} = 20\text{ rad/s}$, and $P = 40.0\text{ W}$ on both sides.

**Predict first (before you run it):** The link is $m = 0.40\text{ kg}$ with its center of mass at $L_{\text{com}} = 0.10\text{ m}$, the payload is $m_{\text{tip}} = 0.50\text{ kg}$ at $L = 0.20\text{ m}$, and the motor sits behind an $N = 6.0$, $\eta = 0.90$ planetary gearbox. Commit to three numbers before the block runs: (1) the holding torque at the horizontal pose, in $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$ — nearer $1$ or nearer $2$; (2) whether the torque at $60^\circ$ is exactly half the horizontal value; (3) whether the motor torque $\tau_{\text{motor}}$ comes out above or below $\tau_{\text{load}}(0)/N$, and why. Two tells that a wrong answer is a mistake rather than a surprise: a horizontal torque near $0.9\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ means the link's own mass at $L_{\text{com}}$ was left out, leaving only the payload's $0.50 \times 0.20 \times 9.81$; and a motor torque larger than the load torque means $N$ was multiplied where it should have been divided.

Size the motor torque $\tau_{\text{motor}}$ required to hold a horizontal single-link robot arm ($m_{\text{link}} = 0.40\text{ kg}, L_{\text{com}} = 0.10\text{ m}, L = 0.20\text{ m}$) carrying a tip payload $m_{\text{tip}} = 0.50\text{ kg}$ at $\theta = 0\text{ rad}$ and $\theta = \pi/3\text{ rad}$ ($60^\circ$) through an $N = 6.0$, $\eta = 0.90$ planetary gearbox.

blocks.text:
import math

def arm_gravity_torque(theta_rad: float, m_link: float = 0.40, l_com: float = 0.10,
                       m_tip: float = 0.50, l_total: float = 0.20, g: float = 9.81) -> float:
    return (m_link * l_com + m_tip * l_total) * g * math.cos(theta_rad)

tau_0 = arm_gravity_torque(0.0)
tau_60 = arm_gravity_torque(math.pi / 3.0)
N = 6.0
eta = 0.90
tau_motor_0 = tau_0 / (eta * N)

assert math.isclose(tau_0, 1.3734, rel_tol=1e-9)
assert math.isclose(tau_60, 0.5 * 1.3734, rel_tol=1e-9)
assert math.isclose(tau_motor_0, 0.254333333, rel_tol=1e-6)
print(f"tau_load(0 deg)={tau_0:.4f} N*m, tau_load(60 deg)={tau_60:.4f} N*m, tau_motor={tau_motor_0:.4f} N*m")
tau_load(0 deg)=1.3734 N*m, tau_load(60 deg)=0.6867 N*m, tau_motor=0.2543 N*m

blocks.x: A timing-belt reduction connects a motor pulley with $Z_{\text{motor}} = 16$ teeth to a joint pulley with $Z_{\text{joint}} = 72$ teeth ($\eta = 0.95$). Compute the gear ratio $N = Z_{\text{joint}} / Z_{\text{motor}}$, the output speed $\omega_{\text{joint}}$ when $\omega_{\text{motor}} = 90\text{ rad/s}$, and the output torque $\tau_{\text{joint}}$ when $\tau_{\text{motor}} = 0.40\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$. Verify $N = 4.5$, $\omega_{\text{joint}} = 20.0\text{ rad/s}$, and $\tau_{\text{joint}} = 1.71\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ ($\pm 10^{-6}$).

items.x: **If your result differs:** Check that the driven pulley tooth count ($72$) is divided by the driving motor pulley tooth count ($16$): $72 / 16 = 4.5$, and multiply $\tau_{\text{motor}} \times N \times \eta = 0.40 \times 4.5 \times 0.95 = 1.71\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$.

[`exercises/02-mechanics.T1.02a/`](../exercises/02-mechanics.T1.02a/) turns this section into a test. `starter.py` holds seven holes: `gravity_torque` (the cosine lever arm, link plus tip), `balance_force`, `gear_ratio`, `gear_output_speed`, `gear_output_torque` ($\eta N \tau$), `mechanical_power` and `reflected_inertia` ($N^2$). Edit it, then run the tests the way CI does:

**29 tests.** The torque is checked at the worked example, at the horizontal maximum and at vertical poses, so a sine where the cosine belongs fails; the balance force is checked at the Skip test's $60\text{ N}$; the belt drive is checked at the exercise's $4.5$, $20\text{ rad/s}$ and $1.71\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$, so an inverted ratio, a multiplied output speed or a dropped efficiency each fail; and the reflected inertia is checked at $N^2$ rather than $N$. The transfer suite runs **the plant's own arm**: the submission's shoulder term must reproduce `plant.gravity_torque`'s difference between the two links at four poses, the folded elbow's full lever arm is checked (the pose that looks vertical is not the zero-torque one), the $2.5\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ clamp is pushed back through an $8{:}1$ belt, and `plant.I1` reflected through $4{:}1$ is $0.128\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$. Five planted faults - `gravity_uses_sine`, `balance_divides_wrong`, `gear_ratio_inverted`, `output_speed_multiplies`, `torque_ignores_efficiency` - each fail the test named for them.

items.x: **The ratio comes from the teeth, in the right order.** The joint pulley is the driven one, so $N = 72/16 = 4.5$; writing $16/72$ gives $0.222$ and every downstream number inherits it.

**A reducer slows and strengthens.** $\omega_{\text{joint}} = 90/4.5 = 20.0\text{ rad/s}$ and $\tau_{\text{joint}} = 0.95 \times 4.5 \times 0.40 = 1.71\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ — speed divided by $N$, torque multiplied by $N$.
**The efficiency belongs on the torque, not the speed.** $\eta = 0.95$ costs $5\%$ of the torque ($1.80\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ without it) and none of the speed.

**Power is the check that the two sides agree.** $\tau_{\text{joint}}\omega_{\text{joint}} = 1.71 \times 20.0 = 34.2\text{ W}$ equals $\eta \tau_{\text{motor}}\omega_{\text{motor}} = 0.95 \times 0.40 \times 90 = 34.2\text{ W}$; if the two differ, the speed or the torque was scaled the wrong way.

**What the suite refuses.** `gravity_torque` raises on a negative mass; `balance_force` raises on a lever arm at the pivot (which balances nothing); `gear_ratio` raises on a zero tooth count; `gear_output_speed` raises on a zero ratio; and `gear_output_torque` raises on a gear efficiency outside `(0, 1]`. Each of those is a `ValueError`.

blocks.x: Inject the `gravity_uses_sine` fault the graded package names, and diagnose it from the two poses in the worked example:

items.x: **Inject:** replace `math.cos(theta_rad)` with `math.sin(theta_rad)` inside `arm_gravity_torque`, leaving the masses, the lever arms and $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$ untouched.

**Symptom:** the horizontal pose now reads $\tau_0 = 0.0000\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ — an arm that hangs out flat and needs no holding torque — while $60^\circ$ reads $1.3734 \times 0.8660 = 1.1894\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ instead of $0.6867\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$, so the printed order is reversed and the motor is sized at $1.1894 / (0.90 \times 6.0) = 0.2203\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ instead of $0.2543\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$.

**Diagnose:** the amplitude $1.3734\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ still appears in the output, just at the wrong angle, so $(m L_{\text{com}} + m_{\text{tip}} L)g$ and the unit chain are correct and only the angle factor can be wrong. Gravity's lever arm is the horizontal distance $L_{\text{com}}\cos\theta$ from the pivot: largest when the link lies along the horizon, zero when it points straight up. A sine factor peaks at $90^\circ$ from the horizontal — the vertical pose, where the arm balances over its own pivot — and that is the one symptom a mass error cannot produce.

**Fix:** put `math.cos` back. Then $\tau_0 = 1.3734\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$, $\tau_{60} = 0.6867\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$, and $\tau_{\text{motor}} = 1.3734 / (0.90 \times 6.0) = 0.2543\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ — the worst-case gravity load the gearbox must hold, which is the number a motor is sized on.

`[Concept: gear_reduction_speed_torque_power_conservation]` A motor pulley ($Z_1 = 20$ teeth) drives a joint pulley ($Z_2 = 100$ teeth). Compute the reduction ratio $N = Z_2 / Z_1$ (tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$).

`[Concept: gear_reduction_speed_torque_power_conservation]` Using the $N = 5.0$ reduction above with efficiency $\eta = 0.92$ and motor torque $\tau_m = 0.50\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$, compute the output joint torque $\tau_{\text{load}} = \eta N \tau_m$ in $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$ (tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$).

`[Concept: gear_reduction_speed_torque_power_conservation]` If the motor spins at $\omega_m = 150\text{ rad/s}$ into the $N = 5.0$ reducer, compute the output joint angular velocity $\omega_{\text{load}}$ in $\text{rad/s}$ (tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$).
`[Concept: gear_reduction_speed_torque_power_conservation]` Why can a gearbox with ratio $N > 1$ multiply torque ($\tau_{\text{load}} = N \tau_m$) **without** violating conservation of energy?

**A.** Because it simultaneously divides angular velocity by the exact same factor ($\omega_{\text{load}} = \omega_m / N$), so mechanical power $P = \tau_{\text{load}}\omega_{\text{load}} = \tau_m \omega_m$ is conserved (minus friction loss).
**B.** Because gears create energy out of steel teeth.
**C.** Because both speed and torque increase by $N$.
**D.** Because torque does not have units of energy.

head: Symptom
Root cause
2-minute fix
rows: Used $sintheta$ instead of $costheta$ for gravity torque when $theta = 0$ is defined as horizontal
Mixed up the angle measured from the horizontal $+x$-axis vs. the vertical $-y$-axis.
Always check $theta = 0$: if $theta = 0$ is horizontal, gravity torque is maximum ($cos 0 = 1$); if $theta = 0$ is hanging straight down, gravity torque is zero ($sin 0 = 0$).
Omitted the link's own mass $m_{text{link}}$ when sizing the shoulder motor
Calculated $m_{text{tip}} g L$ for the payload only and forgot $m_{text{link}} g L_{text{com}}$.
Sum $(m_{text{link}} L_{text{com}} + m_{text{tip}} L) g costheta$ across both link self-weight and payload.
Multiplied speed by $N$ instead of dividing by $N$ on a speed reducer
Inverted the gear ratio definition $N = omega_{text{motor}} / omega_{text{load}}$.
Sanity-check that a speed reducer ($N > 1$) makes the output joint spin **slower** ($omega_{text{load}} = omega_m / N$) and push **harder** ($tau_{text{load}} = eta N tau_m$).
